svg.title: A service chain with a broken return path beside the same chain where both directions traverse the same stateful device
svg.desc: Left panel: client, firewall and server in a row with forward arrows through the firewall, but the return path drawn in red as a curve that bypasses it entirely, so the firewall never sees the reply; the symptom is a completed handshake followed by stalled or reset data. Right panel: the same chain where the return path is forced back through the firewall and IPS, achieved with symmetric routing, policy routing in both directions, VASI or service insertion. A footer lists four ways the return path gets lost: policy routing that only covers the forward direction, asymmetric ECMP hashing, NAT translated sources that nothing routes back, and an off-ramp service node with a single interface that can be entered but cannot hand traffic back.
svg.text: The bottleneck of service virtualisation is the return path
A stateful device only works if it sees both directions. The forward arrow is easy to draw; the return arrow is the design.
BROKEN: RETURN PATH BYPASSES THE CHAIN
client
FW
stateful
server
forward
forward
return goes straight back through the core
the firewall never sees the reply
symptom: SYN passes, handshake completes, data stalls or resets
DESIGNED: BOTH DIRECTIONS ON THE SAME CHAIN
client
VRF USER
FW / IPS
inline, stateful
server
VRF DC
return is forced back through the same device
mechanisms: symmetric routing, PBR in both directions, VASI or service insertion
Four ways the return path gets lost
1. PBR sends forward traffic to the firewall, but the firewall's return route points at the core, not at the client VLAN
2. Asymmetric ECMP: forward and return hash onto different links, so a stateful device sees one direction only
3. NAT translated the source, and the return traffic addresses a pool nobody routes back
4. The service node sits off-ramp with a single interface: it can be entered, but it cannot hand traffic back
